strength.text: When the refill history contradicted her, you told her what it showed, said you were not trying to catch her out, and offered two ordinary reasons people struggle with metformin. That made it safe for her to tell you the truth.

evidence.quote: Metformin is hard on a lot of people's stomachs, and it isn't cheap. What gets in the way for you?
evidence.speaker: learner

important_gap.text: You gave her the HbA1c number and what it means but did not check her understanding. With low health literacy, asking her to tell you in her own words what the result means would confirm it.

transcript.speaker: learner
transcript.text: Good afternoon, Mrs. Alvarez. I'm Priya, a nurse practitioner student working with Dr. Chen. I'd like to hear what's been going on, look at your chart with you, and make a plan together. Does that sound all right?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: That's fine. I'm thirsty all the time and I'm up all night going to the bathroom.

transcript.speaker: learner
transcript.text: That must be wearing you down. When did you first notice it?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: About three months ago. It keeps getting worse.

transcript.speaker: learner
transcript.text: Tell me about a typical day. What do you eat and drink from morning to night?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Whatever's left at the cafeteria, mostly. And my sweet tea, four or five big glasses.

transcript.speaker: learner
transcript.text: Thank you, that helps me. I see metformin on your medication list. How is that going?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Oh, it's fine. I take my metformin every day.

transcript.speaker: learner
transcript.text: Okay. I'm going to pull up your pharmacy refill history so I have the full picture.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: All right.

transcript.speaker: learner
transcript.text: It shows two fills in the last six months. I'm not trying to catch you out. Metformin is hard on a lot of people's stomachs, and it isn't cheap. What gets in the way for you?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: It tears up my stomach, and it's forty dollars I don't always have. I didn't want you to think I wasn't trying.

transcript.speaker: learner
transcript.text: I don't think that at all. Thank you for telling me, because it changes what I'd suggest. I'd like to check an HbA1c, which shows your average sugar over the last three months. Is that okay?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Okay. Is it bad? I'm scared of where this is heading.

transcript.speaker: learner
transcript.text: You look frightened. What are you most afraid of?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: My mother had the sugar too. She was on dialysis before she died. I don't want to end up like that.

transcript.speaker: learner
transcript.text: I'm so sorry about your mother. It makes sense that this scares you. Your HbA1c is 9.2 percent. That's higher than we want, and it fits with the thirst. It is something we can bring down.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Even if I can't take the pills?

transcript.speaker: learner
transcript.text: I'll go over the options with Dr. Chen rather than promise something specific, and I'll tell her about your stomach and the cost. In the meantime, would you be willing to swap some of the sweet tea for water? What feels doable?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: I could do two glasses instead of five.

transcript.speaker: learner
transcript.text: That's a real start. So: you'll cut the tea to two glasses, I'll talk with Dr. Chen about the metformin, and we'll see you back in two weeks. What questions do you have?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: No, I think I understand. Thank you for not making me feel bad.
